items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: When the House resumes on
Tuesday, 5 November the Government intends to progress a number of bills on the

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE

State-owned Energy Companies, Sales—Progress, Costs, and Public Support
1. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green) to the Minister of Finance: Does
he consider that the Government’s Meridi an Energy sale was a failure, given that it
attracted only 62,000 retail buyers, which is only a quarter of the 250,000 forecast?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister
of Finance: No, I do not agree with that. The Meridi an Energy float is, in fact, by value
the largest retail investment in an internal public offering in New Zealand’s history. The
62,000 shareholders mean that Meridian Energy will have the third-largest share register
of all the companies on the NZX when it lists next week. The share float will provide
$1.9 billion in cash for the Government, which we can invest in other public assets
without having to borrow. It will be 86.5 percent New Zealand - owned when it lists,
comfortably meeting the Government’s targ et of 85 percent local ownership. And,
finally, the 250,000 figure that th e member quotes was not a forecast. Treasury thought
it might have to cater for up to that figure for planning purposes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will he now accept that his asset sales programme has failed to
achieve his goal of widespread public ownership, when only 1 percent of New
Zealanders bought into Meridian Energy and the other 99 percent of New Zealanders
did not, because they are finding it hard enough to pay the power bill let alone buy a
power company?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, and I do find it rather unsavoury when a politician who
has been doing his best to sabotage a floa t comes down here and complains about the
number of shareholders who participated in a float. He should look at himself—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That answer now is long enough.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will he now accept that his asset sales programme has failed to
achieve his goal of keeping costs under $120 m illion for all of the privatisations, when
in fact the cost to the taxpayer for just the first two privatisations is now well over $250
million?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I doubt the veracity of the member’s comment, but can I
tell him this: this Government and New Z ealand taxpayers have benefited from these
floats—so far, to $3.6 billion—and if the member  thinks it is that bad, why does he not
just go out there and promise to buy them b ack and borrow the money offshore, or just
print the money?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will he now accept that his asset sales programme has failed to
achieve his goal of raising $5 billion to $7 billi on, given that it is now very clear that it
will not even get near the bottom of the $5 billion to $7 billion band?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, and here we have a member once again, for his own
political gain, trying to cost New Zealand taxpayers money by talking down the value of
these assets, as he has done the whole the way through. Again, there is something
unsavoury when a Government is elected on a policy programme and an individual sets
out to economically sabotage it.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will he now accept that his asset sales programme has failed to
convince New Zealanders that privatisatio n is a good idea, given that the vast
majority—99 percent—did not buy shares in  Meridian Energy, New Zealanders have
consistently opposed the sales in every pub lished opinion poll, and New Zealanders
signed the petition in record numbers for a referendum on asset sales?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, and that is because the New Zealand public is cleverer
than Mr Norman, because they understand that the Government makes choices—it has
to make choices on their behalf. They do not  want to borrow money, they do not want
mad printing money; they want to know that  the Government is running the economy
well. The sad thing that sticks in that me mber’s craw is that this Government was
elected on this policy at the last election.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Who chose to go ahead with the de cision to sell the shares in
Meridian Energy, in spite of all the problems of going ahea d—was it the Minister of
Finance or was it the Green Party? Who was responsible fo r the decision to go ahead
with the sale?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Government makes its decisions. It is quite patently
obvious that the Green Party is not responsible, full stop.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given that it was the Government’s decision to go ahead with
the sale, in very unfavourable circumstances with very poor outcomes, will the Minister
of Finance take responsibility for the abysmal outcome, where only 62,000 people
bought into the company, or about 1 percent of New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Dear oh dear. No. The reality is simply this: it is the most
successful retail initial public offering by value in New Zealand’s history. We have
62,000 retail shareholders, and if the member  wants to look for anybody who wants to
know why there were not more shareholders, he  needs to look in th e mirror at his crazy
1970s-style, socialist, communist central power policy.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he really think it is credible to blame everyone else for the
failure of his asset sales programme, rather than taking responsibility for it himself—I
thought individual responsibil ity was one of the premises of the National Party—and
does he really want to blame it on the Green and Labour parties for presenting a popular
and credible plan that would reduce pow er prices, given th at only 1,700 potential
investors pulled out of Mighty River Power after NZ Power was announced anyway?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is quite patently obvious that the Greens believe in fairy
tales. Their politics around ec onomics are absolutely hope less. This float has been
successful. The Government has raised $3.6 billion. If the member is not just politicking
like his friend on the convention centre, he should pop out and say that he would buy it
back.

2. Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance : Does he
stand by all his statements?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister
of Finance: Yes. In particular, I stand by my stat ement of last evening that the Labour
Opposition has no credibility in criticising the share offer programme, because it has
had the opportunity for months to say it will go and borrow $2 billion from foreign
bankers to buy these assets back, and as far as I know, it has not promised it, the Greens
have not promised it, and New Zealand First has not promised it. It is all crocodile tears,
hand wringing, and politicking from the Opposition.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Which of these statements made by him in the last 24 hours
regarding the Meridian Energy float are correc t: that it was “a success”, that it “met our
objectives” and was “a pretty good outcome”, or that the Meridian Energy float was
“sabotage”?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: If the member had listened to the answer to the primary
question for question No. 1, he would have he ard we listed all the ways in which the
float has been a success—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I listed a series of
quotes and asked the Minister which ones were  correct. That was the simplicity of the
question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I appreciate the simplicity of the question. I think the member is
trying to address the question. If we give him some time, we might well get the answer.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: As I said, it has been a success for all the reasons outlined,
in answer to parts of his question. But in terms of the sabotage issue, the reality is that if
Labour and the Greens were being responsible , more people would have felt confident
about buying shares in Meridian Energy and also Mighty River Power. To that degree,
Labour and the Greens have been sabotaging the public share offers.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Simple question—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: It would have to be.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Especially for you, Gerry. Give n that answer, how can he
claim that the float of Meridian Energy was “a success” but at the same time “it was
sabotaged”?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, I just said. I will try it again a little slower for the
member. It was a success because of the amount of money raised, the 62,000
shareholders, the 86.5 percent New Zealand owne rship, and the fact that it is, by value,
the largest retail inve stment in an initial public o ffering in New Ze aland’s history.
Where it could have been more successful , if the Greens and Labour had not been
deliberately scaremongering, is to have even more shareholders who wanted to invest
for the first time.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Given that he forecast repe atedly that $5 billion to $7
billion would be raised from asset sales and given that Solid Energy is no longer fit for
sale, the Government got $110 million less fr om Mighty River Power than planned, and
the Government is more than $1 billion short on what was forecast for the Meridian
Energy sale, how exactly will his Government make up that shortfall?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Minister of Finance has been saying for some time that
it will be at the lower end of  the $5 billion to $7 billion range, because Solid Energy is
not available for sale. It ju st goes to show how much th ese valuations can move over
time. The good news for investors and the go od news for New Zealanders is that as
these assets are listed on the New Zealand Exchange, they will be valued on a daily
basis.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question again was
exactly—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I heard the question, and the problem is that if the member
wants a specific answer, that is the s upplementary question he should ask. Has the
member got a further supplementary question?

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Given that the polls consistently show that an
overwhelming majority of the public are oppos ed to asset sales and only 14 percent of
New Zealanders were even interested in purchasing Meridian Energy shares, why did he
ignore the clear market signals and proceed with the Meridian Energy float, with the
upshot being that only 1 percent of the populat ion at best, given that a large number are
institutions and trusts—not mum and dad Kiwis—purchased shares?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think I have answered that  question in primary question
No. 1, from Mr Norman, but I am happy to  repeat it for the member because he
obviously did not hear it. It is pretty straightforward. In terms of the very first part of his
question, in terms of the popularity or othe rwise of the share offer programme, the
reality is the New Zealand public has looked at the Government’s economic programme
as a whole. They think it makes sense, and that is why they elected this Government
again in 2011 with all of th at programme laid out. This programme has raised $3.6
billion so far. If the member had any c ourage, he would say that he would buy the
shares back.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Given that 99 percent of Kiwis did not buy Meridian
Energy shares, is his Government now truly the Government for the 1 percent?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: With the greatest respect to the member, he must be able to
do better than that.
State-owned Energy Companies, Sales—Progress and Purpose
3. PAUL GOLDSMITH (National)  to the Minister of Finance : What recent
progress has the Government made in its share offer programme—a nd particularly in
generating money for investing in new public  assets without having to borrow from
overseas lenders?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: on behalf of the Minister
of Finance: I thank the member for that question. The Government is making very good
progress with its share offer programme, which we, of course, put to voters at the last
election. Last night we confirmed the sale of  49 percent of Meridian Energy, which will
raise around $1.9 billion in two instalments. Based on the $1.50 a share issue price, this
is the largest retail investment in an initial public offering in New Zealand’s history.
With 86.5 percent of the shares owned by Ne w Zealanders when Meridian lists on the
New Zealand Exchange next Tuesday, this comfortably meets the Government’s goal of
achieving 85 percent to 90 percent New Zealand ownership.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: How many New Zealanders have invested in Meridian Energy and
how does this compare with the share registers of other New Zealand listed companies?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Some 62,000 investors will receive shares in Meridian
Energy. This means Meridian will have the third largest share re gister on the NZX,
behind Mighty River Power and Contact Ener gy. Overall, 95 percent of retail investor
applications for Meridian shares will receive at least 90 percent of the shares they have
applied for. Meridian attracted a different mix of investors than we saw with Mighty
River Power earlier this year. Demand was strong and broad-based, but overall we saw
retail investors bidding for slightly larger  parcels of shares. Having said that, around
half of all Meridian investors applied fo r 5,000 shares or fewer, so there was strong
demand from smaller investors.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: On behalf of taxpayers how will the Government use the $1.9
billion in proceeds from the Meridian Energy share offer?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The approximately $1.9 billion raised from Meridian
Energy’s two instalment payments will be a llocated to the Future Investment Fund. On
behalf of all New Zealanders, that money w ill be invested in the Government’s public
infrastructure programme, which, in turn , supports thousands of jobs across New
Zealand. Combined with the $1.7 billion in proceeds from the Mighty River Power offer
earlier this year, there will now be almost  $3.6 billion over the two floats that the
Government does not have to borrow to reinvest in new priority public assets. These
include modern schools, new hospitals, ir rigation projects, s upporting KiwiRail, and
helping to rebuild Christchurch. We can do a ll of those things without having to borrow
this money from overseas lenders. And the question is: what would the Opposition do?

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: You borrow from overseas inve stors every week. You borrow
all the time.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: You’ve borrowed more money than anybody else.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What alternative approaches to  the share offer programme are
available?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: There are three main alternatives. One would, of course, be
to not invest in new schools, hospitals, or ultra-fast broadband. I doubt that anybody is
suggesting that. Another option would be to borrow the billions of dollars from overseas
lenders to invest in these new public assets. Some in this House appear to favour that
borrowing option, including the Hon Annette King—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —and Grant Robertson. A third option is promising to buy
back the minority shareholdings  in these energy companie s and borrowing billions of
dollars from overseas banks to pay for th em. But nobody in this House is proposing to
do that, so I can assume only that the oppone nts of this share programme do not have
the courage of their convictions, but I have to say—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That answer will not help the order of this House.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker . As recently as the last day or
so, someone else who has used that phras e has been challenged to withdraw and
apologise for it. Mr Joyce made a direct link between members in this House and a lack
of courage. That is out of order and he should have to withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If the member has taken offence, that is a—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member has taken offence, a nd on that basis I ask the Minister
to stand, withdraw, and apologise to Mr Robertson.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I withdraw and apologise to Mr Robertson.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I also took offence.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Well, it is—[ Interruption] Order! That is not strictly a point of
order. The offence has been apologised for. Any member who was so—[ Interruption]
Order! Any member who was so offended by the remark can now accept the apology
that has been given.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The apology was a
qualified one to only Mr Robertson and not to the House. It pays to listen.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member can stand and withdraw the last part of that remark.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I withdraw—to you, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Thank you. Now, on the basis that Mr Mallard—[ Interruption]
Order! On the basis that—[ Interruption] Order! On the basis that potentially there were
other members who were offended by the Minister’s remark, I am now going to ask him
to stand, withdraw, and apologise without addressing the offence to anybody.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Sorry, is that to Mr Mallard, or to—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would the Minister just stand, withdraw, and apologise for
the remark he made in an earlier answer.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I withdraw and apologise.
Housing, Affordable—Mortgages and Availability
4. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atat ū) to the Minister of Finance : What
reports, if any, has the Reserve Bank had from  trading banks on the effect of loan-to-
value ratio lending limits on housing construction?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister
of Finance : The Reserve Bank advises that it has not received reports from trading
banks on the effect of loan-to-value ratio restrictions on housing construction. I would
not expect to see such reports, given the Reserve Bank’s independence on macro-
prudential policy.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: What impact does he expect loan -to-value ratios to have on the
Government’s housing policy, which claims to  be focused on trying to increase supply,
if, as Warwick Quinn of the Registered Mast er Builders Federation predicts, they result
in 3,000 fewer new homes being built each year?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: That is a difficult statement to reconcile with a statement
made by the Registered Master Builders Fe deration to the Minister’s colleague the
Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and Employment at around the same time, when
it said it was worried there would not be enough apprentices and enough people with
skills to actually build all the houses. So I th ink we need to rationalise where we are at
here: either there are not e nough people around to build all the houses or there are not
enough houses going to be built. I am sure we will resolve that situation.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Can he explain why the Prime Minister said “I can’t for the life of me
see how it will affect home building.” at the same time  as the Reserve Bank is currently
researching the impact on new builds of loan -to-value ratios, or should we give this
statement the same credibility as the Prime Minister’s earlier promise to protect first-
home buyers from the effects of loan-to-value ratios?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: If housing prices are rising, that generally leads to
increased supply over time. The issue is wh ether that supply is happening fast enough.
Given that prices have been rising, it is entirely reasonable to say that more construction
will occur. If the member is saying that will not happen, then he really does need to go
back to Economics 101 and have a chat to the economics lecturers at the time.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Is he concerned that Treasury rubbished the Government’s changes to
KiwiSaver and the Welcome Home Loan scheme, saying they were questionable
spending and would undermine housing affordability, and will he now concede the
changes were a desperate attempt to distract  attention from the damage that his housing
policy is doing to first-home buyers?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, and it is interesting to note that the member himself
said the policies were not big enough. So on the one hand he is citing Treasury
criticism, and on the other hand  he is saying we should do more, which, actually, is not
inconsistent with his previous statements, which have been both in favour and against
loan-to-value ratios. Th e answer to this problem is to have a larger s upply of housing.
That is why the Minister has done the special housing areas and announced 6,000 more
houses to be built in Auckland, which, of course, the Opposition opposes.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Will he admit that the Government’s housing policy is in tatters, with
Treasury criticising recent policy announcements as ineff ective and questionable and
recommending that the Government consid er policies like a capital gains tax and
excluding offshore speculators—policies that he refuses to consider?
24 Oct 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14269

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The member might want to read Treasury’s
recommendations on capital gains taxes, because Treasury is keen to have it on all
houses. The trouble with having it on all ho uses, of course, is that that affects
everybody’s family home. But that is what Trea sury is seeking. If the member wants to
line up with that pol icy, I would welcome his announcemen t in that regard, and I think
everybody on this side of the House would.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Everybody else is wrong!

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: But in terms of capital gains taxes, Mr Twyford, the
situation in Australia is th at they already have one lik e the Labour Party policy, and
their prices are going up even faster.
Sexual Abuse—Measures to Address
5. MELISSA LEE (National)  to the Minister for Social Development : What
recent initiatives has the Government suppor ted to provide better support to those
affected by sexual violence?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: On Tuesday I was
pleased to speak in Auckland at the launc h of a new web portal called The Harbour, a
resource for those who have been affected  by sexual abuse. The Harbour will allow
people to access vital information from a single, trusted source so they do not have to go
to multiple different sites to access the info rmation they need. There is a myriad of
information on the internet and, unfortunatel y, much of it is not correct. The Harbour
includes information on how to access help if you are a victim  of sexual abuse, as well
as information about how to assist if you fear someone may be being abused.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: How is The Harbour a good example of  a whole-of-sector approach to
addressing sexual abuse?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The Harbour is a result of excellent collaboration
between the Government and NGOs. Developm ent of The Harbour has been led by the
Safe Network, and its chief executive, Jacqui Dillon, deserves a real special mention for
this being her initiative and for getting ev eryone on board. The Sa fe Network is an
Auckland-based organisation th at provides treatment for harmful sexual behaviour
alongside the Auckland Sexual Abuse Help Foundation and Rape Prevention Education.
There was a range of other Government agen cies contributing. The Ministry of Social
Development through Family and Community Services and Child, Youth and Family,
the New Zealand Police, the Department of  Internal Affairs, the Department of
Corrections, ACC, the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Hea lth, the Ministry of
Justice, and the Ministry of Women’s Affairs all contributed in some way.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: How does The Harbour work to help prevent sexual violence?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Well, what is a little differe nt is that not only does The
Harbour provide information for victims and their friends and family but also it acts as a
resource for those who fear that they them selves may be at risk of offending. People
concerned about their own behaviour can go to the “I think I’m causing harm” page on
the site to seek information about what is normal behaviour and how they can seek help
if they fear they might have offended or be offending against someone. I welcome this
initiative and I congratulate those who have done it.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: What will the Minister do to  actually fund organisations that
provide services to those affected by sexua l abuse, like Wellingt on Rape Crisis and
Male Survivors of Sexual Abuse Wellington,  which are currently having to consider
cutting services or closing down completely?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We currently have a review  under way of all of those
services, and we are making very good prog ress. I think what happened with the
Auckland helpline and the Auckland Sexua l Abuse Help Foundati on is actually a good

example of real collaborati on across agencies. As I say, we are making progress, and I
think you will see that in due course.
New Zealand Defence Force—Impact of Attrition Rates
6. Hon PHIL GOFF (Labour—Mt Roskill)  to the Minister of Defence : Have
attrition rates in the last year, which reach ed 23 percent in the Navy and 24 percent in
the Army, reduced the capability of the New Zealand Defence Force?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: As the Chief of Defence
Force told the member at the Foreign A ffairs, Defence and Trade Committee on 6
December 2012 and also on 22 June 2013, the New Zealand Defence Force has had no
cut in capabilities. The member is also wo rking with out-of-dat e statistics. The New
Zealand Defence Force attrition rate today is  14 percent, which is below the historic
long-run average and well below the 19 per cent figure under Labour. Both army and
navy attrition rates today are significantly beneath levels reached under Labour.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: When the navy admits that skill and experience levels in critical
trade groups have been seriously degrade d—their words, Mini ster—by the significant
reduction in the number of trained personnel av ailable, why does he keep on pretending
that this has not reduced the navy’s capability?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Because the fact is that it has not. The navy is
actually performing to all the targets that ha ve been set for it by th e Government, and it
is meeting all the outputs that it is contracted to meet by other Government agencies.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: If the navy is meeting all of its targets, why does the navy say in its
latest report that it cannot crew more than f our out of six of its new naval patrol force
vessels—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: What?

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: —cannot crew more than four out of six of its new naval patrol force

items.text: What progress is the Government making in increasing housing supply,

improving the quality of the Government’s  housing stock and gr owing the community
social housing sector?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I am encouraged by the latest

trebling the number of houses that it is going to  build from 300 per year to 1,000 per

accommodation, we have established th e Canterbury Earthquake Temporary

housing stock. Tomorrow I am meeting with th e new Mayor of Christchurch to explore

11. Dr CAM CALDER (National)  to the Associate Minister of Transport : What

items.text: Excellent

2012 we saw a 44 percent decrease in deaths for our 15 to 19-year-olds and a 48 percent

be deadly. I wish everyone across the H ouse and across the country a safe long
weekend, and I hope everyone comes back in one piece.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I move, That the Policing (Constable’s
Oaths Validation) Amendment Bill be now read a second time . The bill is validating
legislation that will deem oaths of office taken by police employees between 13 October
2009 and 13 October 2013 to have been administered as though the persons
administering those oaths had been authorised by the Commissioner of Police. It is a
straightforward amendment involving the inser tion of one new secti on into the Policing
Act 2008. It is to come into force the day after it receive s the Royal assent.
[Interruption] It gives me no great pleasure to be here either.
The background to this bill is as follow s. On 1 October 2008 the Policing Act came
into force. Prior to this under the Police Act 1958 the constable’s oath was taken before
a justice or a commissioned officer of police at the rank of inspector or above. A justice
or commissioned officer of police was not re quired to be specifically authorised to
administer the constable’s oath. However, s ection 22 of the Policing Act instituted a
new procedure for administeri ng the constable’s oath. Unde r the current Act the oath
can be administered only by the commissioner or a person specifically authorised by the
commissioner. In addition, the person admini stering the constable’s oath must be
satisfied that the police employees who are taking the oath have been adequately trained
and are capable of exercising the powers of a constable.
Between 13 October 2009 and 13 Octobe r 2013 the constable’s oaths were
administered to ex-constables who were rejoining the police  by district commanders or
inspectors based in the police districts, w ho had not been formally authorised by the
commissioner. The district co mmanders and inspectors had assumed that they had the
authority to administer the oath. The consta ble’s oaths have now been administered to
the affected police employees by persons fo rmally authorised unde r section 22 of the
24 Oct 2013 Policing (Constable’s Oath s Validation) Amendment Bill 14279
Policing Act, so all affected employees have had full constabulary powers conferred
upon them.
However, uncertainty about conferral of  constabulary powers continues for those
affected police employees who purportedly exercised constabulary powers without the
necessary authority between 13 October 2009 and 13 October 2013. It is very important
that people should have confidence that offi cials are properly inve sted with statutory
powers and that taxpayers shoul d not be obliged to meet th e significant expenses that
would be incurred if all exer cise of statutory powers ta ken by the affected employees
was subject to legal challenge.
The bill will deem the oaths taken by affected  constables to have been administered
as if the persons administering the oath s had been approved by the Commissioner of
Police. It will remove any doubt about the validity of the actions of the affected police
employees and thereby promote certainty and confidence in the acts carried out by
them. The legislation is consistent with th e New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. The bill
does not retrospectively validate actions that could be seen as inconsistent with the New
Zealand Bill of Rights Act.
I have been assured by the Commissioner of Police that steps have now been taken to
make sure that this does not happen again. They are putting in place a system that will
not fully register a constable who has b een undergoing training until the oaths are
checked and it is ensured that the appropria te process has been followed. I thank my
colleagues in the House for their forbearance at having to put through this legislation
under urgency this afternoon. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: For some, I am sure, it will seem quite
unbelievable that we can be he re again—and I do want to em phasise that we are here
again—dealing with a similar matter that we have dealt with before. I will go through
the history of the police oath in a moment, but I just want to say that as much as the
Minister—less so, actually, the Minister—and, indeed, much more so, as Gerry
Brownlee tried to express his faux grumpiness at the police for the situation that we find
ourselves in, I have to say the way he has conducted himself in the House this afternoon
procedurally means that most people were prob ably more inclined to think that it has
been incompetence on that side of the House th at may have actually led us to this place
today.
We can only assume that this is indicative, to a certain degree, of a Minister who has
taken her eye off the ball. We all know  about the concept and importance of
constabulary independence, but that certainly should not mean distancing yourself so far
from your role as Minister of Police that not even your constables  are being sworn in
properly. That is how far constabulary independence has gone today.
For the sake of those listening today, t hough, I want to go back over how we have
come to the point where we are now going thro ugh urgency, in order to rectify an error
in the way that the law has been administered and constables have received their ability
to do their duties under the Policing Act. So let us go back to the background.
The Policing Act of 2008, which was i ndeed passed under Labour, was the
culmination of an incredibly large amount of work. It was conducted in a cross-party
way, because, of course, for matters like the wa y that the police are governed, it is only
right that we get bipartisan support on an issue like that. It took roughly 2 years of
consultation before that bill came to the House.
Before the 2008 Act, the Police Act of 1958 set out how a constable’s oath was
undertaken. That was set out in section 37 of the Police Act 1958. The old law was
more liberal in the way that a constabl e was conferred their power. There was no
specific authorisation required in order to conf er an oath. It could be carried out by any
14280 Policing (Constable’s Oaths Valid ation) Amendment Bill 24 Oct 2013
commissioned officer. That was section 37 of the Police Act 1958—quite liberal in the
way that it set out those oaths.
The Policing Act 2008 was quite different. I want to refer to section 22 of the
Policing Act 2008, which says: “A Police employee may become a constable only by
taking the constable’s oath, in either of the following forms, before the Commissioner
or a person authorised by the Commissioner to  administer the constable’s oath:”. That
was the change that was made in 2008. It was recognised, however, in October of 2009
that that Act was not being appropriately ad ministered, and that was essentially because
people who were not correctly authorised had continued to act in the way that they had
under the old law.
That meant that we had an amendmen t made through the Policing (Constable’s
Oaths Validation) Amendment Act that provided that for the period from 1 October
2008 to 12 October 2009, everyone who was c onferred on oath over that period was
retrospectively covered and their oaths were validated. So that  brings us up to date with
today. That is the history of this saga thus far.
At some point it has been brought to the Minister’s attention, however, that even then
that amendment was not being appropriately applied. I would not mind hearing from the
Minister of Police, when she rises to her feet to make another contribution to the House,
at what point she became aware of this. I would not mind hearing from the Minister—or
from her colleague Judith Collins, who was, I believe, the Minister in charge at the time,
in October 2009. It was her job to ensure that this amendment was then implemented
appropriately across the New Zealand Po lice. Be under no doubt that it was the
Minister’s job then to make sure that this was carried out appropriately.
But what happened instead? Well, we now  know that although that was being done
appropriately within the Police College situ ation, there are 63 ex-constables who have
rejoined the police since 13 October 2009 w ho took their oath before a person not
authorised to administer the oath. How did that  happen? Well, in the old days it used to
be that a superintendent or an area contro ller could administer the oath locally to
someone who was coming back into the police because, of course, they were not
coming back through the Police College. That  was how the old Act allowed that to
happen.
Of course, as I have already outlined, and, in fact, if we go to  section 22 of the
Policing Act, it very clearly states that an oath is to be taken before the commissioner or
before a person authorised by the commi ssioner. “A Police employee may become a
constable only by taking the constable’s oath in either of the following forms, before the
Commissioner”—really clear; that is set out in primary legi slation, and nothing more is
required—“or a person authorised by the Commissioner …”.
So what happened? The Government did not authorise district commanders to carry
out those oaths locally for ex - police office rs who returned. It was pretty explicit,
though, that that was exactly what needed to happen according to the Act. The one thing
that needed to happen, and the Minister needed to ensure was happening, was that it was
either the commissioner who carried out the oath or it was someone authorised by the
commissioner—pretty straightforward.
Why did the Minister not ask who had been authorised to carry out those oaths? Why
did the Minister not make the checks and ba lances to ensure that if they were not
happening through the Police College, it was at l east ensuring that those oaths that were
happening outside the Police College were auth orised? It was a very basic thing, after
reaching the situation that we had got to, wh ere we had to go through urgency, surely, a
Minister who had her eye on the ball with regard to what was going on within the police
would have asked that very question. So that is a signif icant concern for the Labour
24 Oct 2013 Policing (Constable’s Oath s Validation) Amendment Bill 14281
Party. I would like to hear from the Minister why those checks and balances were not in
place.

items.speaker: But let me be absolutely cl ear
items.text: it would be irresponsible of members on this side of
the House—in fact, it would be irresponsible of any party in this House—not to support
this legislation. We need to ensure that t hose 63 officers, in the performance of their

items.text: If only the member who is in terjecting from his seat, Mark

doing today should be taken by the Govern ment as providing a carte blanche for
ramming through legislation under urgenc y or ramming through retrospective

So Mr Mitchell can say that it is only 63 o fficers but, I am sorry, that is 63 police

I want to refer briefly to what Gerry Brow nlee said. It is not my habit to quote the

embarrassing was when the Leader of the House got up and then resumed his seat
without moving the motion that he had got up to move. Then the Minister of Police got
up to begin the second reading debate with her speech and forgot to move the motion
that this be read a second time. What this s a y s  t o  m e  i s  t h a t  w e  a r e  s e e i n g  a  t a w d r y
Government that is not on top of its game. This is a mistake-ri dden Government, and

Anne Tolley, the Minister of Police, said that this was a straightforward amendment.

24 Oct 2013 Policing (Constable’s Oath s Validation) Amendment Bill 14283
that it is OK to get things of fundamental importance wrong. I am really worried that the

made a huge difference. If our crime rate is less than it was before, that is because we

In fact, when I look at the figures that you gave us, they represent a cut in numbers—

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: A few days ago when I first saw the title of this bill
we are debating today I actually assumed it was on my desk by mistake. I saw the top
line and thought: “Why has somebody disinterre d that old thing?”. For a moment I
thought: “Was there a sunset cl ause in that legislation we passed back in 2009 under
urgency?”. Of course there was not. It was a piece of legislation necessary to remedy an
error, and sadly here we are again some 4 years later, once again retrospectively putting
right virtually the same mistake. Clearly that  is an unacceptable situation. It brings no
credit to anyone. It chews up a great deal of time in this Parliament at a time of year
when we have a long Order Paper and after th is only five more sitting weeks. It is a
wholly unsatisfactory situation, but there you are.
The new bill of course, the Policing (Consta ble’s Oaths Validation) Amendment Bill
2013, will sit alongside a bill en titled exactly the same but the last number would be
2009. The Greens will support this bill simply b ecause it would be irresponsible to do
otherwise, and that point has been made by our Labour colleagues.  The situation that
the bill remedies is untenable and cannot be  allowed to stand. I would make the point
that we are supporting this bill of our ow n volition despite some rather over-excited
media commentary, which I saw earlier today,  suggesting what the Greens, and indeed
Labour, have done: “A backstairs deal has be en sewn up to ensure the legislation…”
passes. I would just like to put on record th at neither I nor any of  my Green colleagues
have met with Minister Tolley on the backst airs or anywhere else. It is a nonsense
report. We are supporting this legislation b ecause, as I said, it would be irresponsible
not to.
The situation is untenable. It  is untenable for a number of reasons. We cannot allow
the error to stand. To do so would put 63 serving police officers in a position where they
could be prosecuted for carrying out their duties, which they have done in good faith for
the time since they have been sworn in. If a ny one of us was to pr esent ourselves as if
we were police officers we would clearly be subject to some fairly serious legal
consequence, and that is as it should be. Impersonating a police officer is an extremely
serious offence, and so it should be. Effectiv ely the 63 officers have been, in effect,
impersonating a police constable, and that is  an untenable situation for them. They
could be personally liable for their actions  at any point where they have gone beyond
carrying out activities that a normal person, a civilian, a non-officer would carry out.
They are then vulnerable to being charged personally, and that is simply unacceptable.
The other side of it, of course, is that any of the prosecutions, arrests, or legal
processes that those officers or their activities have stimulated could be deemed invalid.
It could clearly result in ongoing prosecutions  having to halt and convictions having to
be overturned. Effectively some people who committed crimes, people who have
performed criminal activities, could get off,  and could escape just ice if we do not put
this error right. As I say, it would be simply untenable to do otherwise.
I actually enjoyed the hospitality of the Poli ce Association at its dinner last night. I
had to bite my tongue quite hard on a number  of occasions to not reveal the content of
what we would be debating today. I looked about that room and I wondered whether
any of these 63 affected officers were in th at room. In all likeli hood at least some of
them were. It puts them in a very unhealthy situation.
24 Oct 2013 Policing (Constable’s Oath s Validation) Amendment Bill 14285
I think it is worth quoting th e insertion into the Policing Act, section 115A of the
2008 Act, which was inserted as a result of the 2009 legislation. It says: “A Police
employee or judicial officer who has admini stered the constable’ s oath described in
section 22(1) in the period 1 October 2008 and ended with the close of 12 October 2009
is to be treated as having been authoris ed, throughout that period, by the Commissioner
to administer the oath…”. Now we are goi ng to see yet another paragraph inserted
below that, one to remedy this latest oversi ght. One hopes that we will not be back in a
year’s time inserting yet more text into that already much amended Act.
At the time in 2009 when the first mistake was uncovered, I think that the media
commentary—and, indeed, academic commentary—was reasonably benign. It was
accepted that a mistake had been made. People make mistakes. It was a technical error,
a glitch. I think there was cer tainly some reporting, in the New Zealand Herald for
example, and Television New Zealand ran a story on the matter. It was, as I said,
reasonably benign; it was not overly critical. I guess we all recognised that we can make
mistakes. But to make the second mistake—or rather, to make the same mistake twice—
simply smacks of carelessness and lack of attention to detail, and that is completely
unacceptable.
There was an academic study done recently on the use of urgency by this
Government and preceding Governments, and there was an interesting analysis done of
situations where these academics judged the use of urgency to be  justifiable or not
against a set of criteria, and I think “or not” equalled political expediency. The
particular piece of legislation passed in 2009 was deemed to be a justifiable use of
urgency, and arguably today is also a justifia ble use of urgency in order to avoid any
appeals against what may have happened in the interim. It may be justified in that sense,
but it is not justifiable to simply accept that this mistake could have been made not once
but twice.
It is critical that we put this right, but it is unfortunate that a recent citizen
satisfaction survey—as recently as Sept ember of this year , and it was a 10,000
respondent survey so it was a pretty r obust investigation—found that 79 percent of
those 10,000 people reported they  were confident in the c ountry’s police officers. The
survey asked people their views about police, their feelings on how safe they felt, and
what their service experience was when th ey had interactions with the police. The
overall satisfaction with service delivery sat at 83 percent, and given that for numbers of
us our interactions with officers are going to  cost us money—if, for example, we have
been misbehaving in terms of speed limits or  whatever it might be—I think that is a
remarkably high display of confidence, and I believe that is well justified. Our police do
a good job, they do a difficult job, and I believe that for the most part they do it very,
very well.
The repetition of this mistake cannot do other than weaken the public’s confidence in
the police service. It can do not other th an cast doubt on the or ganisation: not on
individual officers necessarily, but certainly on the administration of the police force. It
is most unfortunate that the officers out there—who are work ing very, very hard to do
the right thing, to fulfil the oath that they take in good faith, and doing all the right
things by the public to do their best to keep the peace and ensure public safety—are
being compromised by these administrative errors, which cannot stand.
We heard from the Minister earlier that there will be an internal investigation lead by
Police Commissioner Marshall to discover wh at went on and to ensure it does not
happen again. That is a good thing, and I have the greatest confidence in the
commissioner’s integrity, but I think we n eed to go beyond that. I believe we need an
external inquiry into how these mistakes happe ned and how we can be sure that they do
not reoccur. For that reason, I have today written to the Auditor-General’s office, asking
14286 Policing (Constable’s Oaths Valid ation) Amendment Bill 24 Oct 2013
the Auditor-General under sec tion 16 of the Public Audit Act to undertake an inquiry
into this matter to endeavour to identif y what has happened, why it happened, and how
we can ensure that this situation does not occur and that we do not find ourselves once
again in a year’s time passing legislation under urgency to fix something that ought
never to have happened. With that point I wi ll end my speech, but I will seek leave to
table a letter that I have today sent to the Auditor-General. I do seek that leave now.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to take a
call on this, the second reading—notwithstanding th at it is actually the first reading—of
the Policing (Constable’s Oaths Validation) Amendment Bill.
This is retrospective legi slation being passed under ur gency, and in almost every
other case New Zealand First would be totally opposed to it for those two reasons alone.
The fact that this House is being required to  dispense with both the first reading and the
Committee stage of this bill is further reason for us to oppose it under normal
circumstances, as is the reality that th ere will be no public submissions and no
examination by a select committee. However, this is not a typical case, and the
Government’s reasons for bringing this bill—an d bringing it in the manner in which it
has—are not typical either. We realise that , and we understand that  a part of being a
constructive party of Opposition sometimes requires us to put pragmatism ahead of
pedantry. We believe this is one of those occasions.
We could choose to oppose this bill and th e manner in which it is traversing this
House on principle. We could decry the Gove rnment for trampling on the constitution,
riding roughshod over established convention, violating the essence of democracy, and
tearing down the ramparts of due lawmaking process. In almost any other case we
would and in any other case we would be justified in so doing and, indeed, it would be
our constitutional duty to do so. But this is not an ordinary matter, and the nature and
realities of the issue that this bill seeks to address dictate that  we are compelled by
reasons of pragmatism to view  this bill and this proces s through a different lens. As
such, New Zealand First does endorse the use of  this process in this case, and we will
therefore support the passage of this bill.
This bill is a short, simple instrument of legislation. Its passing into law will have no
great ramifications for the New Zealand nation.  In fact, it will go  unnoticed by ordinary
people as they go about their everyday lives. However, the consequences of not passing
it, even in this somewhat ab rupt and irregular fashion, do  have the potential to cause
much upset and disquiet.
This bill corrects what is in reality nothing more than a technical error in the process
of the reswearing-in of a small number of returning former police officers. These are
24 Oct 2013 Policing (Constable’s Oath s Validation) Amendment Bill 14287
officers who have been police constables in the past, who have been sworn officers, and
who have carried out police duties in that cap acity. They have left the service of their
own volition and then chosen to return. In doing so, it is required that they be resworn.
However, for a small number of them —some 63 in total—sometime during the
period in which they were out of the police force, the rules changed around who was
and who was not authorised to  carry out that reswearing. Th is has meant that for some
of them—the 63 officers referred to—the oath taken when they re-entered the force was
administered by a person not authorised to administer it unde r those particular
circumstances. This bill corrects that anomaly and it is necessary that it does so, because
if the anomaly is not corrected, the officers in question are, technically, not sworn police
constables.
The implications of this are that the ar rests they have made  over the period, since
they returned to the force, and all other pol ice duties are technically  illegal. It does not
require a great intellect to deduce from this  that many people who have been rightly
arrested, brought before the courts, found gui lty and convicted, a nd subjected to the
penalties of the State may find themselves with the legal avenue by which they may
have those convictions overturned. We would find ourselves having to let people out of
jail, despite the fact th at they are, in fact, guilty of the crimes for which they have been
incarcerated. This would of course be ridi culous. The only winners would be criminals
and, of course, lawyers, who would have a field day and—dare I sa y it—a rather large
pay day as well. And we cannot have that.
New Zealand First understands and accepts that in some circumstances—on some
rare, few occasions—circumstances dictate th at normal due process must be dispensed
with, in the best inte rests of the greater good. This, we f eel, is one such case. I reiterate
that it is a simple, straightforward, transpar ent, and necessary matter to advance this
change, and for those reasons  we will be supporting the bi ll, even though under normal
circumstances we would vociferously oppose it  on the basis of urgency and truncated
process.
I do not intend to take up any more of the time of the House, or give the legal
vultures any more time to circle, before clos ing by saying again th at New Zealand First
supports this bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I take a call on this very important—

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It is a split call. I understand I have 5 minutes, which I will fill
to the full. This is a very important ma tter and we should not take it lightly. This
Parliament should not take it lightly. My starting point is the principle of the rule of law.
The rule of law starts with this House a nd its conduct and the laws that it passes, and
when Parliament, with the power of the peopl e, passes laws that bind and constrain the
people, we require all those with authority under the law to act properly and within the
authority conferred by this Pa rliament. If there is one gr oup of people for whom acting
within their powers is absolutely crucial and is the sine  quo non of their job, it is the
police. Their job is to uphold the law, not any law but our  criminal code. Their job is to
uphold the laws that affect our conduct a nd our behaviour. There is an underlying
morality to our criminal code, and we exp ect our police to uphold it. But because we
confer on them very coercive powers—the pow ers to arrest and detain, to deprive of
liberty—we require them to act within their powers.
This House has the job of passing laws, but this House has another job too. We elect
members of the executive—the Ministers who are in charge of departments and agents
of the Crown. Parliament, having voted funding, having voted money, requires the
executive to do its job to ensure that mone y, having been appropriated, is used for the
purposes for which it is appropriated, but al so that those who act  under their executive
delegation do so within the powers and the authority conferred by this Parliament,
which itself acts in the name of the people of New Zealand. So when we find, not for a
first time but for a second time, that some of those people within whom we charge the
most serious powers—powers that can constrain the liberty of an individual—are acting
without the appropriate author ity and power required by this Parliament, we should sit
up, take notice, and act with an appropriate level of sobriety.
It is for that reason that it does pay for this House to take some time to pay some
attention to it, and to give it scrutiny. Th is is a mistake that has happened. I do not
accept it when people say that the police o fficers themselves should be somehow held
responsible because they should know the la w. Those police officers are reliant on their
superiors exercising their pow ers and authorities approp riately, and that has not
24 Oct 2013 Policing (Constable’s Oath s Validation) Amendment Bill 14291
happened. It is not just a matter of 63 consta bles not having been sworn in properly but
everything they have done in the execution of  their duty, without this bill, would be
invalid. That goes far and wide. That is not  just arresting people. It is not just
intervening in domestic disputes. It is everything they have done. Had anybody known
about it and had there been so me resistance, had those consta bles been assaulted in the
course of their duty, because that is a common occurrence with our police force,
unfortunately, and had that then gone befo re the court, then the police officers
themselves would have been left with no protection at all.
I take my hat off to this Minister for bringing this bill back to the House. But the
question must go really to what her predecessor was or was not doing. How is it that the
mistake had been made once, but now it is be ing made a second time. That is where we
can talk about the police, pa ss this bill, shore up their authority, and validate those
actions. That is the sensible thing to do, but there must be some accountability. It is the
Minister who has failed to act. It is the Mi nister who provides oversight. It is the
Minister who ought to be as king the questions. And, having  made the mistake once, I
would have thought that any self-respecting Mi nister of Police woul d then continue to
ask what has happened. Has the law been co mplied with? When that police Minister
then becomes a Minister of Justice—a senior  Minister and sometime  heir apparent to
the throne of the National Party—that failure runs even deeper. So we support the bill,
but let us not deny that this is a very serious situation.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I move, That the Policing (Constable’s
Oaths Validation) Amendment Bi ll be now read a third time . The Policing (Constable’s
Oaths Validation) Amendment Bill is valida ting legislation that will deem oaths of
office taken by police employees rejoining the New Zealand Police between 13 October
2009 and 13 October 2013 to have been administered as though the persons
administering those oaths had been author ised by the Commissioner of Police. It
removes uncertainty about th e conferral of c onstabulary powers for those police
employees who purportedly took the constabl e’s oath between 13 October 2009 and 13
October 2013.
This Government is committed to effectiv e public administration and to supporting
our front-line police constables. This bill achieves these objectives by removing the risk
that the actions of affected police employees can be challeng ed for the sake of it. The
bill does not affect redress in the unlikely event that it is necessary for those whose
rights might genuinely have been breached. Th is bill is a straightforward administrative
provision that fixes a techni cal matter directly and cleanl y. I thank the members of the
House for their forbearance. I thank the me mbers of the House for their support and
their responsible actions here this afternoon. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I wish to use my time in the third reading of the
Policing (Constable’s Oaths Validation) Amendment Bill to really clarify what I think
are the quite justifiable ques tions that Opposition members are asking here. This is not
14292 Policing (Constable’s Oaths Valid ation) Amendment Bill 24 Oct 2013
an attempt to politicise a situat ion that clearly absolutely needs to be rectified. There is
no question. That is why it is being passed unanimously through this House. I can see
Mr Sabin muttering over there with quiet, silent  rage. He must be quite upset that he
does not get to use his 10 minutes. Perhaps Mi nister Tolley might let him have his full
10 minutes for that.
I just want to clarify that  Labour is not liberally sp reading the blame across our
police force, over the fact that we are havi ng to deal with this issue today—of course
not. In fact, rightly so, we have acknowledged the work that the police do on behalf of
all of us in our communities. It is an incred ibly tough job in that we constantly ask of
them to reinforce the notion that no matter how  much disrespect th ey are treated with,
they continually treat others with constant respect. That is  what we ask of our police
officers daily, and, by and large, they do an  absolutely fantastic job for us. We
acknowledge that.
What we are saying here today is that, yes,  an error was made ba ck in the way that
the original legislation, passed in 2008, wa s enacted functionally, on the ground. That
was rectified in 2009. Usually, of course, under normal circumstances it probably would
be unfair to say that the Mini ster of Police should have overs ight of every single little
individual issue that has been implemented in the 2008 Policing Act. Under normal
circumstances, that would be a fair comment  for the Government to make. But this was
not a usual circumstance.
The House went into urgency in 2009 to make a specific  change, and retrospective
legislation was passed to cove r the fact that for a period one part of the 2008 Act was
not implemented correctly. That should have been a flag then to the Minister—in an
area where she probably would not usually have functionally ope rated any oversight—
to just ask some questions. That does not  interrupt the concep t of constabulary
independence, which is an incredibly important  principle, just as is the independence of
the judiciary—very important principles. Bu t we cannot blur the line between needing
to maintain constabulary independence and ensuring proper accountability for a
Minister who has oversight of the operational day-to-day functions of the police.
Because a set of unusual circumst ances did arise, I think it is  fair to say that at that
point the Minister should have said: “Well, look, OK, this law has been passed. Please,
in my next briefing or update with the commissioner, at least demonstrate to me that the
proper authorisations have b een administered for those who are now giving out those
oaths.” Just one question—one brie fing. That is all it would ha ve taken, and that is not
unusual. Once a piece of legislation has b een implemented, it is not unusual for a
Minister to ask for an update on implem entation—absolutely not. Because this is one
very specific question, it woul d not have taken much to as k for that. So I do want to
highlight that, yes, constabulary independenc e is incredibly important, but I see that
used as an excuse time and time again, when actually what we are asking for is simple
ministerial accountability. We need to make sure it is applied correctly.
In my first address I spoke briefly about  some of the things that are going on
generally within the police right now. I think it is only right to mention that the Police
Association members are at their annual conf erence as we speak, and it was a real
pleasure to join with them last night at that event. But I would not want to leave the
House with the view that the 63 officers since 2009 who have come back into the police
force somehow demonstrate this amazing recr uitment drive and increase in policing
numbers. In fact, those 63 returning officers represent more, in terms of numbers, than
what the police force has grown by in its enti rety since 2009. In f act, we have had an
increase of only 52 police officers, sworn st aff, since 2009. Putting that into context,
that is under a Government that promised New Zealand that we would have functionally
24 Oct 2013 Policing (Constable’s Oath s Validation) Amendment Bill 14293
one staff member per 500 Ne w Zealanders. That means we  should have had an extra
252 front-line officers, if that Government stuck to its word. But it has not.
What the Government may claim is that, sure, we have got only 52 more officers,
according to the annual report, but, of cour se, there are all the non-sworn staff and the
various roles that they play. Let us be ve ry clear about what has happened to non-sworn
staff, who perform an incredibly important job on behalf of the policing family. They
may not be sworn staff, but  sworn staff see how importa nt and know how important
their role is. They are the one s who do all of the work that often frees up police to do
that front-line policing—those patrols that we expect of  the police, and which the
Minister claims they are doing more of. There are 234 fewer non-sworn staff now than
in 2009. That means the burden of those tasks is now falling squarely on sworn
officers—234. That has not just been because people have left. Let us be absolutely
clear. There was a restructure in 2012, wh ich was extraordinarily unsettling for the
police generally—not just for th e non-sworn staff. The sworn staff felt acutely the fact
that the people who were supporting them in their work were restructured out of their
jobs, asked to take early retirement, or asked to apply again in cities that were quite a
distance even from where they  were performing their duti es at that time. I know it
affected a number of police officers in po lice stations deeply and the volunteers who
worked for them.
Of course, we need to remember that there are a number of volunteers who work
with our police force. I had the pleasure of knowing one of Ne w Zealand’s longest-
serving police volunteers, Ia n Jenkins, who served with the New Zealand Police in
Morrinsville—from memory, for over 30 years— and did an incredibly  stellar job. We
cannot ignore that it is not just sworn po lice officers who play a role in keeping our
communities safe; it is all the people who s it around them. I know that the police would
want me to mention that, and want me to mention how unsettling that period was.
Mr Goff has already talked about what th at has meant regionall y, and I think it is
important to focus on it. When we use these statistics at a national level, it is easy to
lose sight of what it means for a community. But in Counties Manukau 104 fewer police
personnel is going to have a significant im pact on a community like that, where, of
course, our expectation is not that the poli ce simply play a role of respond, inquire, and
arrest. We, for a long time, have asked the po lice to form a much bigger role than that.
In fact, their own commissione r has significantly changed th e focus of the police with
the notion of prevention first. We applaud Prevention First as an initiative. It is fantastic
but it does require police to be able to manage their file and case loads of their major
criminal investigations. Unless they are able to  do that, it is very hard to implement this
wider notion of prevention first.  It is harder to ask them  to do some of those early
interventions and preventative work when they are doing just the day-to-day file
management that they are required to do as part of their front-line duties.
We all lose when we have a police force that  is feeling those kinds of pressures on it.
That is bearing out in some of the survey wo rk that we have seen where the police have
said that only a quarter of our cops claim to be fully engaged in their work, and the
number that are leaving is significant. In 2013 the averag e monthly resignations have
doubled—have doubled—since 2008. Clearly, thes e are police officers who are feeling
the pressure of having less support around th em, the increasing demands, and the fact
that their budgets are barely keeping up with inflation, and th is is bearing out in their
ability to do the job that they signed up to via the oaths that we are now fixing today.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: I rise once more with feeling, the second time in an
hour or so, to express support for this Policing (Constable’s Oaths Validation)
Amendment Bill, albeit, dare we say it, grudging support. All of us would rather not be
here debating this particular retrospective fix-it for a failed process. It is unfortunate that
we are here once again, and we hope it is for the last time in this context.
The bill is, of course, the Policing (Constable’s Oaths Validation) Amendment Bill. I
think it is worthwhile to reflect just for a moment on the nature of that oath that our
police officers take as the last step towa rds becoming fully fledged constables and
before they step into the role and actually  start exercising those powers and duties of a
police officer. I will not read the oath di rectly. That would seem wrong, because I think
people earn the right to recite this oath, so I will paraphrase slightly. Essentially, it says
that the constables—the recruits, the officer s coming into the role of constable—swear
to faithfully and diligently serve, effectively, the Sovereign, the Crown. This is because,
of course, the police force is ultimately answerable not to the Government of the day but
to the Crown—to the head of State, not to th e head of the Government. That is entirely
as it should be, and I think it is worth recalling that.
24 Oct 2013 Policing (Constable’s Oath s Validation) Amendment Bill 14297
The constables go on to say that they will  serve without favour or affection, malice,
or ill will. They say they will, to the be st of their power, keep the peace, prevent
offences against the peace, a nd, to the best of their skill and knowledge, perform all the
duties of the office of constable according to law. So that is a very profound statement.
That is a very powerful, unequivocal statement.  There are no weasel words within it. It
is something that is clearly a very solemn oath, entered into sole mnly. It is a great
shame that for the 63 officers, the integr ity of that moment—that oath—has been
compromised by the administrative errors that  we are seeking to retrospectively put
right today.
Again, the point has been made that the pow ers of a constable are significant. They
have the power to detain, the power to arre st, the power to stop vehicles and search
vehicles, and the power to search individu als in some limited situations. There are
significant powers involved, such as a right  to use reasonable fo rce that goes beyond
what a normal citizen can do. So these are not trivial matters. Th ese are not trivial
issues, and it is important that we acknow ledge the importance and the significance of
what we are doing today, and, indeed, the significance of the errors that have been made
over several years, which we are now putting right.
Similarly, it is worth just refl ecting on what a constable ac tually is. I think that the
common understanding would be that cons tables are those sturdy men and women
whom we see out on the front lin e, in the patrol cars, and on the street. But, in fact,
every police officer remains a constable,  from the Commissioner of Police on down.
Every officer is a constable, so we are talking about the entire police force. They never
relinquish those powers and dutie s and responsibilities while they are serving. As the
principal legislation says, a constable is an “employee who—(a) holds the office of
constable [and is appointed under whicheve r Act]; and (b) includes a constable who
holds any level of position w ithin the New Zealand Police”. So it is not only, shall we
say, the front line or the new recruits who are affected by this but, in fact, every serving
police officer.
I think it is worth reflecting on the fact there are at least 63 returning officers we are
talking about whose swearing-in  has been effectively invalidated by the error. I am
speculating here, but I think we can safely assume, though, that at least some of those
63 returning officers would have some degree of seniority and would have some rank.
So not only have they been performing th eir own duties but they would have been
directing other officers, other units, to carry out duties, which, again, makes the problem
even more severe. Effectively, the orders th ey have been giving, th e instructions they
have been giving to less senior officers, could be invalid, and that just creates all sort of
a rat’s nest that we really do not want to s ee untangled. It is important that through this
legislation we put it right and validate what has been done.
So I think that in the absence of a Committ ee stage for this bill, we clearly have not
paid much attention to the substance of the bill. I have to say that it is a model of
brevity. The explanatory note is ac tually longer than the bill. It consists of four clauses.
It has a title, a commencement date, it identifies the principal Act, and then it has a short
paragraph that will be inserted into the principal Act, the Policing Act of 2008, which
says simply that “A Police employee who has administered th e constable’s oath
described in section 22(1) in the period that commenced on 13 October 2009 and ended
with the close of 13 October 2013 is to be  treated as having been authorised,” to
administer that oath. That is the bill in its entirety. It is a very small bill, but what it does
is actually important and significant, and we should attend to that.
I made the point earlier that I had written to the Auditor-General, seeking an inquiry
from that office into how these mistakes o ccurred and how we can ensure that they do
not occur again. I think it is worth just co mmenting that I am appealing to the Auditor-
14298 Policing (Constable’s Oaths Valid ation) Amendment Bill 24 Oct 2013
General under section 16 of the Public Audit Act, which is headed “Performance audit”.
Specifically, that section says: “The Audito r-General may at any time examine—(a) the
extent to which a public entity is carrying out  its activities effectively and efficiently:”,
and clearly there has been an effectiveness deficit here. It goes on to say that the
Auditor-General may also examine “a public entity’s compliance” with its statutory
requirements, and clearly that goes right to the heart of what has occurred here, back in
The section goes on to talk about “a lack of  probity or financial prudence”. Clearly,
there is not the least suggestion that the police have in any wa y transgressed against
those parts of this section of the Public  Audit Act. It is very much about the
effectiveness, the efficiency, and the comp liance with statutory obligations, and under
those particular provisions I am writing and appealing to the Auditor-General to pick up
this inquiry.
It may well be, and the expectation clearly is , that the responsibility for these errors
will be seen to lie with the senior administrati on of the police force, but clearly it is also
possible that some responsibility  may be found to rest with the Minister of Police or,
indeed, with this Parliament. Each of us as parliamentaria ns may need to bear some
responsibility, and that is fine. That is as it may be, and if that is the finding of the
inquiry, then so be it.
The point is really that it is not a witch- hunt. It is not seeking simply to assign blame
for its own sake; it is actually to ensure  that we do understand. Clearly, there was a
process failure here on at least two occasions—serious failures of process, serious
failures to fulfil what could be seen, on the face of it, to be the quite straightforward
obligation to make sure that this was got right. It has not be en got right, so the intention
of an inquiry must be to uncover how this  happened and to be as sure as we can
possibly be that this does not occur again.
So with those words I will end my comment ary, and I say again that we support this
legislation. Nobody is happy about it, but it would be simply untenable not to see this
retrospective legislation go through. Thank you.

ensure that people who have made these mist akes are held accountable, and that it is

bringing these things to th e House. What I would like  to say to members on the

House rises, it would be really interesting, especially the two former professional police
officers who have served our co mmunity well, if they call her aside and say: “Minister
Tolley, how are you going to ensure that we do not have three strikes? What are you
going to do?”. Is there any advice that Mr  Mitchell or Mr Sabin, having been police
officers themselves, could give Minister To lley on ensuring that pr ocesses are put in
place and that this issue is fixed? Those members will not respond, but I will make this
observation. I suspect that fo r the 63 sworn staff who have  had this hanging over their
heads, it would not be pleasant. Because you always lie awake at night and go “Hang on
a minute. If I have done something and it is  unlawful technically, am I going to end up
in the cart?”. That is a natural human r eaction. You always sit there and just wonder
“Well, it will not be the bosses who get it in the neck because I was the person who”—
for instance—“effected the arre st.” If that arrest, as eff ected, is now deemed to be
unlawful, it is not the commissioner or certain ly the Minister or any of the people on
that side who would end up in the dock; it is the sworn policeperson who has acted with
the best intentions.
So the question is where the buck stops. I say to Miss Tolley and Miss Collins that
the buck stops with them. All we seek in this House—

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: I mentioned in my second reading
contribution on this Policing (Constable’s Oaths Validation) Amendment Bill that the
passing under urgency of retrospective validating legislation is, absolutely, a clearly less
than perfect situation. I th ink that all members in th e House would acknowledge and
accept that. But from time to time, for a variety of very good reasons, such a measure is
required. We do not do it lightly. This is one of those occasions.
Notwithstanding the small element of polit ical ping-pong that has occurred this
afternoon, I want to thank members from acro ss the House for their solid contributions
and their understanding of the situation, because  none of us are pleased to be doing this
in this way on this afternoon. On this side of the House we suppor t the police, and we
do so with enthusiasm, notwithstanding the oc casional mistake. I support this bill and
